section_summary: This section begins with a statistical analysis showing that, despite a fall in dollar value, the physical volume and relative importance of United States war-material exports to Japan remained high in 1938, especially petroleum, machinery, metals, and aircraft. Most of the section consists of congressional and public correspondence urging an embargo or other restrictions on supplies to Japan, together with State Department replies explaining its aeronautical-export policy and the absence of statutory authority to prohibit scrap-iron exports. A substantial group of memoranda concerns Chinese picketing and longshoremen’s refusal to load Japanese vessels at Oregon ports, the resulting diplomatic approaches, and the Department’s decision not to intervene. Other documents address the Nine-Power Treaty, proposed neutrality legislation, World Peace Foundation resolutions, and public appeals against aiding Japanese aggression in China.

subfiles.title: Statistical analysis of United States war-material exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Analyzes the value, volume, and composition of American exports useful for Japanese war-making during January-November 1938.
subfiles.summary: The statement reports that the value of war-material exports to Japan fell from about $157 million in 1937 to $142 million in 1938, but declined much less sharply than other American exports to Japan. It argues that lower commodity prices, rather than reduced physical volume, account for the decline. Petroleum, machinery, iron and steel, nonferrous metals, aircraft, and automobiles dominated the trade, while items legally classed as arms and ammunition formed only a small proportion.

subfiles.title: Tydings transmits Caleb Winslow’s letter
subfiles.about: Forwards a constituent’s protest about sales of war supplies to Japan and requests a reply suitable for transmission.
subfiles.summary: Senator Tydings sends Caleb Winslow's letter and asks the Secretary of State to note and return it with a reply.

subfiles.title: Caleb Winslow protests supplies to Japan
subfiles.about: Asks whether the government is discouraging sales of scrap iron, munitions, and gasoline to the Japanese Army.
subfiles.summary: Winslow calls continued American supply of Japan foolish because it helps Japan wall off China, citing Walter Judd.

subfiles.title: Hull replies to Tydings about Winslow’s protest
subfiles.about: Returns Winslow’s letter and supplies the Department’s statement on exports of war materials to Japan and China.
subfiles.summary: Hull suggests Tydings give Winslow the enclosed State statement on scrap iron, munitions and gasoline exports to Japan.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to A. C. Barnshaw protest
subfiles.about: Directs researchers to another file for Barnshaw’s protest against scrap-iron shipments and Japanese bombing of Americans.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference (393.115/3968): A. C. Barnshaw's December 25, 1938 protest against scrap iron shipments and Japanese bombing of American civilians.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to presidential inquiry on aircraft exports
subfiles.about: Points to a presidential memorandum asking whether aircraft-related exports to Japan could be reduced.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to the President's December 10, 1938 memorandum asking whether aircraft exports to Japan could be curtailed.

subfiles.title: Hinshaw forwards a constituent petition
subfiles.to: The President of the United States
subfiles.about: Forwards a petition from constituents opposing American support for Japan’s invasion of China.
subfiles.summary: Representative Hinshaw sends the President a petition from constituents.

subfiles.title: Petition against participation in Japanese aggression
subfiles.to: The President of the United States
subfiles.about: Urges every practicable measure to end American traffic in materials that supports Japan’s war in China.
subfiles.summary: Petition invokes the Nine-Power Treaty and Kellogg Pact, says American commerce makes the US a partner in destroying Chinese civilians, and asks measures to end the traffic.

subfiles.title: Hull replies to Hinshaw’s petition
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the petition and sends copies of the Department’s statement on exports to China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hull encloses twelve copies of the Department statement for Hinshaw's constituents.

subfiles.title: Church requests fifty copies of the Far Eastern statement
subfiles.about: Requests fifty copies of the Department’s statement for answering constituent communications about arms exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Church asks Hull for fifty copies of the Far Eastern statement for constituent correspondence.

subfiles.title: Hull sends Church fifty statements
subfiles.about: Fulfills Church’s request for fifty copies of the Far Eastern statement.
subfiles.summary: Hull acknowledges Church’s March 1 request. The Department encloses fifty copies of its statement concerning the Far Eastern situation.

subfiles.title: Vermont Secretary of State acknowledges Department statement
subfiles.about: Thanks Moore for sending the Department’s statement on arms exports to China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Vermont Secretary of State Myrick thanks Moore for the statement on arms exports to China and Japan.

subfiles.title: Wilkins asks permission to circulate Moore’s letter
subfiles.about: Requests permission to share a State Department letter with the American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression and other interested persons.
subfiles.summary: Wilkins seeks Moore's consent to circulate his November 28 letter on munitions and war materials more widely.

subfiles.title: Moore authorizes use of his November letter
subfiles.about: States that the Department has no objection to circulation of its November 28 letter.
subfiles.summary: Moore has no objection to Wilkins using the Department's November letter.

subfiles.title: Walsh forwards Norton Kent’s inquiry
subfiles.about: Requests advice on how to answer a constituent asking about shipments of munitions to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Senator Walsh forwards Norton Kent's letter, asking suggestions for a reply.

subfiles.title: Kent asks Walsh about munitions shipments
subfiles.about: Asks whether anything is being done to stop American shipments of munitions to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Kent asks Senator Walsh what is being done about shipments to Japan.

subfiles.title: Hull answers Walsh’s referral
subfiles.about: Returns Kent’s letter and provides the Department’s statement for possible transmission.
subfiles.summary: Hull returns Kent's letter and encloses a statement on munitions exports to China and Japan.

subfiles.title: Lodge forwards Norton Kent’s inquiry
subfiles.about: Seeks the Secretary’s comments on a duplicate inquiry from Norton Kent about munitions shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Lodge forwards Kent's letter from the Boston University physics department, asking Hull for comments.

subfiles.title: Kent asks Lodge about munitions shipments
subfiles.about: Asks whether the United States is acting to stop shipments of munitions to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Kent asks Senator Lodge what the government is doing about shipments to Japan.

subfiles.title: Welles replies to Lodge on export policy
subfiles.about: Explains the Department’s aeronautical-export policy and supplies supporting statements and reports for Kent.
subfiles.summary: Welles encloses the Department's statement, the Munitions Board's report and a January 12 press release; the noncooperating company agreed to comply, so all aeronautical exporters follow the policy against supplying forces bombing civilians.

subfiles.title: Jones thanks Moore for considering foundation resolutions
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Moore’s response to World Peace Foundation resolutions and receipt of the Department’s export statement.
subfiles.summary: Jones thanks Moore for saying the trustees' February 11 resolutions will be considered, and acknowledges the March 1 export statement.

subfiles.title: Moore responds to World Peace Foundation resolutions
subfiles.about: Promises careful consideration of the foundation’s resolutions and encloses the Department’s export statement.
subfiles.summary: Moore thanks Jones for the World Peace Foundation resolutions, assures careful consideration and sends the statement on exports to China and Japan.

subfiles.title: World Peace Foundation submits policy resolutions
subfiles.about: Transmits resolutions advocating an end to supplies for Japan, military preparedness, and broader presidential discretion under neutrality legislation.
subfiles.summary: The trustees declare continued American supply of Japan’s war in China intolerable and call for material sacrifice to end it. They also support adequate American preparedness and reaffirm a 1935 position favoring presidential discretion over embargoes and trade restrictions. Jones invites Hull to use the resolutions as he considers advisable.

subfiles.title: Charge slip for file 894.24 enclosures
subfiles.about: Records the temporary charging or circulation of enclosures from file 894.24.
subfiles.summary: The page is an administrative charge slip containing dates, numbers, and clerks’ notations. It contains no substantive policy discussion.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Japanese concern over neutrality legislation
subfiles.about: Points to a memorandum of conversation on Japanese business interest in prospective American neutrality legislation.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference (894.6363/326): De Friest's February 14 conversation on how new neutrality legislation might affect Japanese business interests.

subfiles.title: Hackworth advises on scrap iron and the Nine-Power Treaty
subfiles.about: Recommends telling Senator McNary that scrap-iron exports do not violate the Nine-Power Treaty and cannot be prohibited under existing legislation.
subfiles.summary: Hackworth advises a concise reply to McNary: a treaty violation could not be sustained and no law prevents or authorizes preventing the shipments.

subfiles.title: McNary forwards Logan’s argument on scrap iron
subfiles.about: Requests State Department views on an Oregon lawyer’s contention that scrap-iron shipments to Japan breach the Nine-Power Treaty.
subfiles.summary: McNary sends John Logan's letter asking Hull to evaluate the claim that munitions or scrap iron shipments violate the Nine-Power Treaty.

subfiles.title: Logan argues that scrap-iron exports violate treaty obligations
subfiles.about: Argues that allowing scrap-iron exports to Japan violates the Nine-Power Treaty and undermines American aid to China.
subfiles.summary: Logan describes Northwest longshoremen refusing to load scrap iron at Astoria, Marshfield and Portland and argues the treaty and Open Door require action against such shipments.

subfiles.title: Hull rejects the treaty argument against scrap-iron exports
subfiles.about: States that scrap-iron exports do not violate the Nine-Power Treaty and cannot be prohibited under current law.
subfiles.summary: Hull says the treaty cannot sustain Logan's argument and no legislation prohibits or authorizes prohibiting scrap-iron exports.

subfiles.title: Church requests fifty additional statements
subfiles.about: Asks for fifty more copies of the Department’s statement on the Far Eastern situation.
subfiles.summary: Church refers to the earlier correspondence filed under 894.24/612. He requests an additional batch of fifty statements for distribution.

subfiles.title: Welles sends Church additional statements and licensing totals
subfiles.about: Provides fifty statements and current figures for licensed arms exports to China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Welles sends Church the copies and licensing totals for arms to China and Japan from July 1, 1937 through March 18, 1939, with blanks left as values change weekly.

subfiles.title: Welles asks Hamilton to draft a reply
subfiles.about: Directs Hamilton to draft an appropriate response to Mr. and Mrs. Baker.
subfiles.summary: Welles notes that he does not remember the Bakers. He asks Hamilton to prepare a suitable reply for his signature.

subfiles.title: The Bakers urge an end to war-material sales to Japan
subfiles.from: Madeleine H. Baker and Walter Baker
subfiles.about: Calls for a rapid halt to American shipments of weapons and other war materials after the writers viewed Walter Judd’s lecture and films.
subfiles.summary: The Bakers, citing Judd's descriptions of Japanese brutality, urge stopping exports of weapons, aircraft, tanks and scrap iron to Japan.

subfiles.title: Welles replies to Walter Baker
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the Bakers’ views and encloses the Department’s statement on shipments to China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Welles tells Walter Baker the Department welcomes public opinion and encloses its standard statement on war-material shipments.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs legal assessment of Oregon picketing
subfiles.about: Concludes that the Department has no proper role in Oregon picketing unless international law or agreements are infringed.
subfiles.summary: Ward holds the Oregon picketing incidents were resolved and give no basis for action; Ballantine may tell Kase informally if it recurs.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Kase about Oregon vessel picketing
subfiles.about: Records the Japanese Embassy’s presentation of information about Chinese picketing of Japanese ships loading scrap iron in Oregon.
subfiles.summary: Kase gives Ballantine an informal memorandum on Astoria and Portland incidents and suggests State contact Oregon's governor; Ballantine notes some difficulties appear settled.

subfiles.title: Chronology of picketing at Oregon ports
subfiles.about: Chronicles Chinese picketing and longshoremen’s work stoppages affecting ships loading scrap iron at Astoria, Coos Bay, and Portland.
subfiles.summary: Chronology of picketing of the Norway Maru at Coos Bay and planned picketing of two other ships, Japanese consul approaches, contemplated port closures, and a Portland demonstration and longshoremen's strike.

subfiles.title: Second conversation with Kase on Oregon picketing
subfiles.about: Records Kase’s submission of an updated chronology and Ballantine’s view that no departmental action was yet warranted.
subfiles.summary: Kase provides a new memorandum repeating the March 6 chronology plus later events; Ballantine says the facts do not call for State action but he follows developments.

subfiles.title: Updated chronology of Oregon vessel obstruction
subfiles.about: Updates the record of Chinese demonstrations and longshoremen’s refusals to load Japanese-connected vessels through March 14.
subfiles.summary: Updated chronology: demonstrators obstructed food delivery to the Norway Maru, Astoria ended scrap-iron storage, an arbitrator ruled against longshoremen, and Portland officials say the federal government should act.

subfiles.title: Hamilton reports refusal to involve State in Portland dispute
subfiles.about: Records Hamilton’s explanation to McNary that State Department intervention in the Portland labor dispute would be counterproductive.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton tells McNary Welles and the Division decided State should not enter the Portland dispute; an authoritative statement on scrap iron should come from Justice.

subfiles.title: Background and proposed response to McNary on Portland disturbances
subfiles.to: Sumner Welles and other Department officials
subfiles.about: Reviews Japanese, Oregon, and Labor Department approaches and recommends against State Department intervention.
subfiles.summary: Memo summarizes Kase's March 6 approach and the legal view that no action is appropriate absent an international-law infringement; suggests McNary or Justice address the absence of a scrap-iron prohibition.

subfiles.title: McNary seeks assistance after Oregon governor’s telegram
subfiles.about: Records McNary’s request for possible federal assistance in ending Chinese demonstrations and longshoremen’s refusal to load scrap iron.
subfiles.summary: McNary reads Hamilton Governor Sprague's telegram warning Portland's port might close and asking State to warn local authorities that interference endangers Japan relations; the Department will respond.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Oregon-picketing memoranda to Tokyo
subfiles.about: Sends the embassy copies of memoranda concerning picketing of Japanese vessels at Oregon ports.
subfiles.summary: Secretary forwards March 6 and 15 conversation records on Oregon picketing to Tokyo to keep the ambassador informed.

subfiles.title: Havenner forwards Chinese American Citizens Alliance protest
subfiles.about: Requests the Department’s position on an appeal to stop credits and war-material shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Havenner forwards a Chinese American Citizens Alliance protest on civilian bombing in China and the contradiction of selling scrap iron to Japan, asking the Department's attitude.

subfiles.title: Hull explains policy to Havenner
subfiles.about: Describes the aeronautical-export policy, reports the cessation of arms-export licenses to Japan, and explains that scrap iron cannot be restricted under current law.
subfiles.summary: Hull sends the statement and reports; the whole aircraft industry observes the policy against supplying countries bombing civilians, no arms licenses for Japan sought or issued in two months, but law gives no authority over scrap iron.

subfiles.title: Welles asks Hamilton to answer World Peace Foundation letter
subfiles.about: Requests a draft reply to the latest World Peace Foundation communication.
subfiles.summary: Welles asks Hamilton to draft a reply for his signature to the World Peace Foundation.

subfiles.title: Jones sends resolutions to Welles
subfiles.about: Sends the World Peace Foundation resolutions, highlighting the resolution against continued supply of Japan.
subfiles.summary: Jones sends Welles the resolution on war materials for Japan, authorizing any use the Department advises.

subfiles.title: World Peace Foundation resolutions
subfiles.from: Trustees of the World Peace Foundation
subfiles.to: U.S. Department of State and the public
subfiles.about: Calls for ending war-material supplies to Japan, maintaining American preparedness, and granting the President flexible neutrality powers.
subfiles.summary: World Peace Foundation trustees condemn supplying Japan's China war, accept possible American economic sacrifices, support preparedness and reaffirm 1935 endorsement of broad presidential discretion over embargoes.

subfiles.title: Welles acknowledges Jones’s resolutions
subfiles.about: Thanks Jones for the resolutions and reiterates that their subjects are receiving careful consideration.
subfiles.summary: Welles acknowledges Jones's March 20 letter and February 11 resolutions, noting the issues are under careful review.

subfiles.title: Church requests seventy-five more statements
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the previous shipment and asks for seventy-five additional copies of the China-Japan war-material statement.
subfiles.summary: Church thanks the Acting Secretary for fifty copies and asks for seventy-five more.

subfiles.title: Hull sends Church seventy-five statements
subfiles.about: Transmits the requested seventy-five additional copies of the Department’s statement.
subfiles.summary: Hull sends Church seventy-five copies of the statement on war-material exports to China and Japan.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to proposed Manchukuo steel purchase
subfiles.about: Points to a memorandum concerning a proposed $11 million American steel purchase for construction in Manchukuo.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference (895.60 Manchuria/15): Hornbeck's talk with Lamont on a Japanese proposal to buy US Steel steel through Guaranty Trust for Manchukuo.

subfiles.title: Lewis thanks Yost for export information
subfiles.about: Thanks Yost for his April 4 response concerning exports of war supplies to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Lewis briefly acknowledges receipt of Yost’s letter. He expresses appreciation for the information about war-supply exports to Japan.

subfiles.title: Lewis asks Hull about American support for Japan
subfiles.about: Asks whether the United States supplies more than half of Japan’s imported war needs and whether that aid can be reduced.
subfiles.summary: Lewis cites an American Committee for Non-Participation circular naming Stimson and asks Hull to verify its claims on American supplies and consider action.

subfiles.title: Yost replies to Lewis with export statement and arms definition
subfiles.about: Provides the Department’s statement and a pamphlet defining arms, ammunition, and implements of war.
subfiles.summary: Yost sends Lewis the Department's statement and the pamphlet International Traffic in Arms with the President's May 1, 1937 proclamation defining controlled war matériel.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference for file 894.24/631
subfiles.about: Directs users from file 894.24/631 to file 811.34/1002.
subfiles.summary: This is a minimal cross-reference slip. It contains only the originating and destination file numbers and no substantive text.

subfiles.title: Harter forwards Foster’s petition and asks about current exports
subfiles.about: Requests comment on an Ohio petition and asks whether aircraft and munitions exports have stopped while oil, gasoline, scrap iron, and other materials remain freely available to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Harter forwards Foster's petition and asks Hull to confirm the distinction between direct military exports and unrestricted commodities usable for war.

subfiles.title: Foster sends anti-aggression petitions
subfiles.about: Transmits signed petitions from Elyria residents opposing American commerce that aids Japan’s war against China.
subfiles.summary: Foster reports universal opposition in his community to commercial assistance for Japan; no one refused to sign, mostly at church meetings.

subfiles.title: Elyria petition for non-participation in aggression
subfiles.from: 106 residents in and around Elyria, Ohio
subfiles.about: Demands a policy stopping shipment to aggressor nations of goods usable by their armed forces and calls for peaceful aid to China.
subfiles.summary: Elyria petition condemns use of American aircraft, gasoline and munitions in bombing Chinese cities and urges non-participation in aggression and an immediate halt to shipments; 106 signatures.

subfiles.title: Hull replies to Harter on exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Explains the policy discouraging aeronautical exports to countries bombing civilians and reports that no arms-export licenses to Japan had recently been requested or issued.
subfiles.summary: Hull sends Harter copies of the Department statement, Munitions Board report and January 12 press release; all aeronautical exporters comply, and no Japan arms licenses were sought or issued in two months.

subfiles.title: Beatrice Wright advocates an embargo on war materials
subfiles.about: Argues that Japan’s dependence on American machinery and lubricating oil gives the United States powerful leverage for an embargo.
subfiles.summary: Beatrice Wright cites Janeway on Japan's dependence on American machine tools and lubricants, links trade with Japan to Axis expansion, and urges an embargo before the balance shifts.

subfiles.title: Welles acknowledges Wright’s embargo appeal
subfiles.about: Thanks Wright for her views and sends the Department’s statement on exports to Japan and China.
subfiles.summary: Welles assures Wright her observations will receive careful consideration and encloses the standard export statement.
